title: Cost, Scale and Reliability
tagline: The bill and the outage arrive together. Plan for both.
story: The assistant works, so traffic grows, and two things arrive on the same day: a finance review of the token bill and a 429 storm that nobody planned for. Cost, capacity and reliability pull on each other. Caching and routing cut spend, quotas shape what you can send, and every retry or failover has a price in tokens, latency or stale state.
oneLiner: Find where the tokens go, buy capacity that fits the traffic shape, and fail in ways you chose in advance.
youWillLearn: Trace where tokens are spent and rank the levers: caching, routing, output caps, compression and batch
Tell the three kinds of Azure 429 apart and explain why a 429 can appear below quota
Enforce limits per consumer at an API Management AI gateway with token limits and token metrics
Compare Standard, Priority, provisioned (PTU), Batch and Flex, and size PTUs from a traffic profile
Choose retries, circuit breakers, hedging, fallbacks, regional failover or degradation by failure type
Write SLIs and SLOs for an LLM application and plan capacity against them

flashcards.front: List the main places an LLM app spends tokens.
flashcards.back: System prompt and tool definitions on every call, retrieved context, re-sent conversation history, output including hidden reasoning tokens, agent loops with tool results, and retries.

flashcards.front: Which cost metric beats cost per token for an agent, and why?
flashcards.back: Cost per successful task. A cheaper model can need more steps, retries or longer outputs, so per-token price hides the real cost.

flashcards.front: Why does a naive chat that re-sends full history cost grow faster than linearly?
flashcards.back: Input at turn k carries all earlier turns, so cumulative input grows with the square of the turn count. Twenty 500-token turns re-send 105,000 tokens.

flashcards.front: What did FrugalGPT report for LLM cascades?
flashcards.back: A cascade matched the best single LLM with up to 98% lower cost, or beat GPT-4 by 4% at equal cost, on 2023 benchmarks and prices.

flashcards.front: What are the Azure model router modes and defaults?
flashcards.back: `Balanced` (default, cheapest within about 1% to 2% of best quality), `Cost` (about 5% to 6%) and `Quality`. Version 2025-11-18 updates in place.

flashcards.front: Name the three causes of an Azure OpenAI 429.
flashcards.back: Quota exceeded, system capacity throttling, and a temporary rate-limit adjustment on Standard. Compare `x-ratelimit-limit-tokens` with your assigned TPM to spot the third.

flashcards.front: How does Azure's TPM check treat `max_tokens`?
flashcards.back: It counts prompt plus `max_tokens` (plus `best_of`) up front. A `max_tokens` of 4,000 consumes 4,000 tokens of limit even for a 200-token answer.

flashcards.front: How does Anthropic's OTPM treat `max_tokens`?
flashcards.back: It counts actual output only, so a high `max_tokens` costs nothing against OTPM. Cache reads also do not count toward ITPM for most models.

flashcards.front: What status codes does APIM `llm-token-limit` return?
flashcards.back: 429 when the per-minute rate is exceeded and 403 when the token quota is exceeded.

flashcards.front: What does `estimate-prompt-tokens` do in `llm-token-limit`?
flashcards.back: It is required. `true` estimates prompt tokens in advance from the request schema. `false` uses actual usage from the model response. Streaming always estimates.

flashcards.front: State the PTU sizing formula.
flashcards.back: `Normalized TPM = peak RPM x prompt tokens x (1 - cache rate) + output-to-input ratio x peak RPM x response tokens`. PTUs = that / input TPM per PTU, rounded up to the increment.

flashcards.front: Why is PTU not always cheaper at scale?
flashcards.back: Capacity is held and billed whether or not requests arrive. Quota and reservations do not guarantee capacity, and spiky or small traffic leaves capacity idle.

flashcards.front: What is PTU spillover?
flashcards.back: Overflow that returns a non-200 such as 429 is routed to a standard deployment in the same resource, for all requests or per request with `x-ms-spillover-deployment`.

flashcards.front: What do Batch deployments trade for a 50% discount?
flashcards.back: A 24-hour completion target, no real-time SLA and a separate enqueued-token quota. They suit evaluation, enrichment and other work nobody waits for.

flashcards.front: How is Azure Flex processing different from Batch?
flashcards.back: Per-request `service_tier: "flex"` with a synchronous API at about 50% off, but no SLA. It is preemptible, so 429 can mean no capacity and 408 means raise the timeout. Preview.

flashcards.front: What is Azure Priority processing's latency promise?
flashcards.back: A target stated as p50 per 5-minute window, for example 99% above 80 tokens per second for some models. It is a target, not a per-request guarantee. It shares quota with standard.

flashcards.front: List the OpenAI guidance for retrying 429s.
flashcards.back: Treat `Retry-After` as a minimum plus a small random delay, otherwise use exponential backoff with jitter, cap attempts and total time, and never retry quota or billing errors.

flashcards.front: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
flashcards.back: Capped backoff alone leaves clients retrying in clusters. Jitter spreads retries in time and reduces the total number of calls.

flashcards.front: When do hedged requests pay off, and what did The Tail at Scale report?
flashcards.back: For cheap, idempotent calls with long tails: send a duplicate after about the p95 delay and take the first reply. A BigTable benchmark cut p99.9 from 1,800 ms to 74 ms for about 2% extra requests.

flashcards.front: What does an APIM circuit breaker return when tripped?
flashcards.back: A 503. Rules are `failureCondition`, `tripDuration` and `acceptRetryAfter`. Rules are approximate across gateway instances and unavailable in the Consumption tier.

flashcards.front: Does Foundry fail over between regions automatically?
flashcards.back: No. Build two resources in two regions. Approximate RTO is minutes for hot/hot, 30 minutes to 2 hours for hot/warm and 2 to 8 hours for hot/cold.

glossary.def: Tokens per minute and requests per minute. The two quota dimensions that most LLM endpoints enforce, each per model and deployment or per organization.
HTTP status for too many requests. Can mean quota exceeded, capacity throttling or a temporary limit cut. Often carries `Retry-After` or `retry-after-ms`.
Provisioned throughput unit. Reserved model capacity billed whether or not requests arrive, with its own quota and sizing rules.
Routing overflow from a provisioned deployment to a standard deployment in the same resource when the provisioned one returns a non-200 such as 429.
A pay-as-you-go tier with a latency target stated as p50 per 5-minute window. Not a per-request guarantee.
A preview per-request tier at roughly Batch prices on a synchronous API, with no SLA and preemptible capacity.
Asynchronous processing at about 50% off with a 24-hour completion target. For work nobody is waiting on.
A single endpoint that picks an underlying model per request, trading cost against quality. Azure offers Balanced, Cost and Quality modes.
Try a cheap model first and escalate to a stronger one when a check says the answer is not good enough.
Random delay added to a backoff interval so many clients do not retry at the same moment.
A rule that stops sending traffic to a failing backend for a trip duration. In APIM a tripped backend returns 503.
A duplicate request sent after a delay near the p95 latency, taking whichever reply arrives first. Cuts the tail at the cost of extra load.
Recovery time objective and recovery point objective: how long recovery may take and how much data loss is tolerable.
The allowed unreliability implied by an SLO, for example 43.2 minutes per 30 days at 99.9%.
A front door for model traffic that applies token limits, metrics, caching, safety and routing. In Azure it is built on API Management.
Serving a reduced but acceptable result, such as a smaller model, a shorter answer or a cached one, when full capacity is not available.

claims.text: On GPT-5.6 and later a cache write costs 1.25x and a read 0.1x the uncached input rate, so one write plus nine reads costs 2.15x versus 10x uncached.
Anthropic 5-minute cache writes cost 1.25x and 1-hour writes cost 2x, and these multipliers stack with Batch pricing.
Azure model router modes are Balanced (default, within about 1% to 2% of best quality), Cost (about 5% to 6%) and Quality, and the current version 2025-11-18 updates in place.
Azure model router context window equals the smallest underlying model, routing reads text only, and caching helps only when consecutive requests reach the same model.
FrugalGPT reported an LLM cascade matching the best single LLM with up to 98% cost reduction, or beating GPT-4 by 4% at equal cost, on 2023 benchmarks.
LLMLingua reports up to 20x prompt compression with little loss on GSM8K, BBH, ShareGPT and Arxiv-March23.

Azure's 429 table lists rate limit exceeded, system capacity throttling and a temporary rate-limit adjustment on Standard (visible by comparing x-ratelimit-limit-tokens with assigned TPM), plus a fourth row for max_tokens estimates that inflate counted tokens.
Azure RPM follows TPM at 6 RPM per 1,000 TPM for older chat models and 1 RPM per 1,000 TPM for o3 and o4-mini.
Azure's TPM check counts prompt plus max_tokens plus best_of up front, and RPM is enforced over 1 or 10 second windows.
Anthropic OTPM counts actual output only, and cache reads do not count toward ITPM for most models; at an 80% hit rate 2,000,000 ITPM handles 10,000,000 input tokens per minute.
OpenAI limits are RPM, RPD, TPM, TPD and IPM per organization and project; 429 slow_down and 503 server_is_overloaded can carry Retry-After.
APIM llm-token-limit returns 429 when the rate is exceeded and 403 when the quota is exceeded, estimate-prompt-tokens is required, streaming always estimates, and counters are per gateway.
When APIM estimates tokens each image counts up to 1,200 tokens, and concurrent requests can briefly exceed the limit.
llm-emit-token-metric allows 5 custom dimensions per policy, 100 unique values per dimension and 1,000 active time series per namespace, and silently discards data beyond that.

Azure Priority processing states latency as p50 per 5-minute window, for example 99% above 80 TPS for gpt-5.6-sol and gpt-6-sol, set on the deployment or per request with service_tier, using the same quota as standard.
PTU capacity is held and billed whether or not requests arrive, quota and reservations do not guarantee capacity, and cached tokens do not consume PTU capacity.
The PTU sizing example (3,400 input TPM per PTU, ratio 8, increment 5) gives 105.88 so 110 PTUs for 1,000 RPM, 200-token prompts and 20-token responses, and 76.47 so 80 PTUs at a 50% cache rate.

Spillover sends non-200 overflow from a provisioned deployment to a standard deployment in the same resource, per request with x-ms-spillover-deployment, and is not supported for Azure DeepSeek or Meta Llama.
Azure Global Batch and Data Zone Batch cost 50% less than Global Standard with a 24-hour target and a separate enqueued-token quota.
Azure Flex processing is preview, 50% off, has no SLA, shares quota with Standard, and from 2026-09-25 unsupported models return 400.
OpenAI Batch API is 50% off, uses a .jsonl file with a unique custom_id, one model per file and a 200 MB upload limit.
OpenAI advises treating Retry-After as a minimum plus a small random delay, capping attempts and total time, never retrying quota or billing errors and counting SDK retries.
In a Google BigTable benchmark hedged requests cut p99.9 for 1,000 keys from 1,800 ms to 74 ms with about 2% extra requests.

An APIM backend has one circuitBreaker rule with failureCondition, tripDuration and acceptRetryAfter, a tripped backend returns 503, rules are approximate across instances and unavailable in the Consumption tier.
APIM backend pools hold up to 30 backends with round-robin (default), weighted or priority balancing, and lower priority groups are used only when higher ones are tripped.
Foundry does not provide automatic failover; approximate RTO is minutes for hot/hot, 30 minutes to 2 hours for hot/warm and 2 to 8 hours for hot/cold.
Azure Front Door can distribute traffic across API Management instances in multiple regions, each routing to Azure OpenAI endpoints in its region.
Azure Monitor metrics AzureOpenAITimeToResponse and AzureOpenAITTLTInMS measure TTFT and total latency for Azure OpenAI deployments.
